authoredPrompt: This figure presents the same red-black tree three times, stacked as parts (a), (b), and (c), with black nodes drawn as filled black circles bearing white numerals and red nodes as light gray circles with black numerals. In all three the root is 26, its left child 17 and its right child 41; 17 carries 14 and 21, and 41 carries 30 and 47. Below those sit 10 and 16 under 14, 19 and 23 under 21, and 28 and 38 under 30, with 7 and 12 under 10, 3 under 7, 15 under 16, 20 under 19, and 35 and 39 under 38. Part (a) hangs a small black rounded box labeled "NIL" from every empty child slot and prints a small numeral beside each key-bearing node giving its black-height, 3 at 26 and 17, 2 at 41, 14, 21, 30, and 10, and 1 at each of the rest. Part (b) redraws the tree with all of those NILs collapsed into one large black circle labeled "T.nil" at the bottom center, reached by curved edges from every empty slot and by a single long curve arcing over the top of the tree from the root's parent pointer; the black-heights are gone. Part (c) omits the leaves and the root's parent entirely, leaving only the numbered internal nodes. Running the eye down the three parts holds the structure fixed while the drawing convention changes, from fully explicit leaves to the compact form.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between drawing conventions: switch among explicit NIL leaves, shared T.nil sentinel, and omitted leaves, and the same numbered tree remains aligned while leaf pointers appear, collapse, or disappear, showing that the representation changes while the red-black tree structure does not.
- Click for black-height checking: click any internal node, and every path from that node to descendant NIL leaves highlights with its black-node count, making the equal black-height invariant testable.
- Hover for color-rule violations: hover over a red node, and its children are outlined while a pass/fail indicator appears, showing why red nodes must have black children.
authoredContext:
A red-black tree is a binary search tree with one extra bit of storage per node: its color, which can be either RED or BLACK. By constraining the node colors on any simple path from the root to a leaf, red-black trees ensure that no such path is more than twice as long as any other, so that the tree is approximately balanced. Each node of the tree now contains the attributes color, key, left, right, and p. If a child or the parent of a node does not exist, the corresponding pointer attribute of the node contains the value NIL. We shall regard these NILs as being pointers to leaves (external nodes) of the binary search tree and the normal, key-bearing nodes as being internal nodes of the tree. A red-black tree is a binary tree that satisfies the following red-black properties: 1. Every node is either red or black. 2. The root is black. 3. Every leaf (NIL) is black. 4. If a node is red, then both its children are black. 5. For each node, all simple paths from the node to descendant leaves contain the same number of black nodes. Figure 13.1(a) shows an example of a red-black tree.
As a matter of convenience in dealing with boundary conditions in red-black
tree code, we use a single sentinel to represent NIL (see page 238). For a red-black
tree T , the sentinel T:nil is an object with the same attributes as an ordinary node
in the tree. Its color attribute is BLACK, and its other attributes—p, left, right,
and key—can take on arbitrary values. As Figure 13.1(b) shows, all pointers to NIL
are replaced by pointers to the sentinel T:nil.
We use the sentinel so that we can treat a NIL child of a node x as an ordinary
node whose parent is x. Although we instead could add a distinct sentinel node
for each NIL in the tree, so that the parent of each NIL is well defined, that approach would waste space. Instead, we use the one sentinel T:nil to represent all
the NILs—all leaves and the root’s parent. The values of the attributes p, left, right,
and key of the sentinel are immaterial, although we may set them during the course
of a procedure for our convenience.
We generally confine our interest to the internal nodes of a red-black tree, since
they hold the key values. In the remainder of this chapter, we omit the leaves when
we draw red-black trees, as shown in Figure 13.1(c).

discrepancies: The default rendering places a large control panel to the right, so the source figure itself is substantially reduced in size rather than appearing as a clean full-width textbook replacement.
Panel (a) labels, NIL boxes, and black-height numerals are much smaller than in the source screenshot and are borderline hard to read at the rendered inline size.
The shared T.nil sentinel curves in panel (b) are only approximate: the fan of arcs is denser/more symmetric and the large outer/root-parent arc is routed differently from the source.
Panel spacing and vertical proportions differ from the source, especially around panel (b), making the middle tree appear more compressed relative to the sentinel and neighboring panels.
evaluation.notes: The tree topology, node colors, NIL conventions, and three-panel concept are accurately represented, but the default layout makes the figure and labels much smaller than the source and the sentinel arcs are not visually matched exactly.
action_items: Reduce or collapse the right-side UI by default, or give the SVG more horizontal space so the three source panels render at a readable textbook scale.
Increase the font size and/or visual scale of panel (a) black-height numerals, node labels, and NIL boxes so they are comfortably legible inline.
Refine the panel (b) curved NIL-to-T.nil links to more closely match the original routing, including the distinctive large outer arc from the root parent pointer.
Adjust vertical spacing between panels and within panel (b) to better match the source proportions.
